flashcards.q: Why doesn't 100% line coverage guarantee your tests catch regressions?
flashcards.a: Coverage instrumentation only tracks whether a line executed, not whether the test asserted anything meaningful about the result. A test with zero assertions gets the same coverage credit as one with a precise assertion -- Martin Fowler's 'Assertion-Free Testing.'

flashcards.q: What is a 'mutant' in mutation testing, and what does it mean for a mutant to be 'killed' vs 'survived'?
flashcards.a: A mutant is the program with one small deliberate code change (a mutation operator applied once). Killed = a test failed against it (good, your tests noticed). Survived = every test still passed despite the behavior change (bad, an undetected regression).

flashcards.q: What is the mutation score formula?
flashcards.a: killed mutants / (total mutants - equivalent mutants). Directly measures whether tests detect actual behavior changes, unlike coverage which only measures execution.

flashcards.q: What is an equivalent mutant, and why can't tooling fully automate detecting them?
flashcards.a: A mutation that's syntactically different but behaviorally identical to the original under every input -- no test could ever kill it. Detecting equivalence in general is undecidable (Rice's theorem), so it requires human triage.

flashcards.q: What's a realistic mutation score target, and why not 100%?
flashcards.a: 70-90%, not 100% -- equivalent mutants can never be killed by any test, so chasing 100% wastes engineering time on an impossible target.

flashcards.q: Roughly how expensive is a naive full mutation testing run compared to the underlying test suite's runtime?
flashcards.a: Commonly 10-100x the suite's own runtime, because every mutant requires a full test suite rerun -- a 2-minute suite generating 500 mutants naively costs hours of CI compute.

flashcards.q: What starting mutation-score threshold does PIT's own guidance recommend for a legacy codebase, and why not higher?
flashcards.a: Start at 70%, ratchet up over time. Mandating 80%+ on day one against a codebase with pre-existing weak tests recreates the same Goodhart's-Law failure that broke coverage-as-a-target.

flashcards.q: How does StrykerJS's incremental mode make mutation testing tractable in PR-gated CI?
flashcards.a: It caches prior mutant results in reports/stryker-incremental.json and only re-mutates/re-tests code changed since the last run -- reported real-world reduction from roughly 30 minutes to under 2 minutes on typical PRs.

flashcards.q: How does PIT use existing coverage data as an optimization?
flashcards.a: It skips mutating lines with zero test coverage -- a mutant there would trivially survive (no test even reaches it), so that outcome is already known from a plain coverage report, saving a full test-rerun for a certain result.

flashcards.q: Name mutmut, PIT, and Stryker's respective ecosystems.
flashcards.a: mutmut: Python (mutates AST, reruns pytest/unittest). PIT/pitest: JVM -- Java, Kotlin (mutates bytecode). Stryker: StrykerJS for JS/TS, Stryker.NET for C#.

flashcards.q: A mutant flips `age >= 18` to `age > 18` and survives every test. What does this reveal about the test suite specifically?
flashcards.a: No test case exercises the exact boundary value (age == 18) -- every existing test is strictly above or below 18, where both operators agree. Only a test at exactly the boundary can kill this mutant; more non-boundary tests won't help.

flashcards.q: What is the practical production pattern for running mutation testing in CI without blowing up build times?
flashcards.a: Incremental/diff-based mutation testing on every PR (gates only changed code) plus a full whole-codebase sweep on a nightly/weekly schedule as a dashboard signal, not a merge gate -- scoped to business-critical modules, not the entire repo.
